claims: A client may be relieved of tax liability if they meet the requirements under section 6015(b)
Under section 6015(b), a joint return must have been made
Under section 6015(b), there must be an understatement of tax attributable to erroneous items of the spouse
Under section 6015(b), the requesting spouse must not have known, and had no reason to know, of the understatement when they signed the return
Under section 6015(b), it must be inequitable to hold the requesting spouse liable for the deficiency
Under section 6015(b), the requesting spouse must elect the benefits of this subsection within the prescribed time frame
Having no involvement in the spouse's business may support a claim that the requesting spouse did not know and had no reason to know of disallowed deductions
The burden of proof lies with the requesting spouse to establish the elements for relief under section 6015(b)

verdicts.why: Section 6015(b) provides relief if all elements are met.
Section 6015(b)(1)(A) requires a joint return for the taxable year.
Section 6015(b)(1)(B) requires understatement attributable to erroneous items of one spouse.
Section 6015(b)(1)(C) requires requesting spouse did not know and had no reason to know of understatement.
Section 6015(b)(1)(D) requires it be inequitable to hold requesting spouse liable.
Section 6015(b)(1)(E) requires election within 2 years of collection activities beginning.
T.C. Memo. 2009-201 and 2007-219 show no business involvement supports 'did not know' element.
Sources show burden rests with Commissioner to prove spouse had actual knowledge of understatement.

claims: The claimed value of the conservation easement exceeds the correct value by more than 200%
A claimed value exceeding the correct value by more than 200% constitutes a gross valuation misstatement
A 40% penalty applies to the portion of the underpayment attributable to the overvaluation of the conservation easement under I.R.C. § 6662(h)

verdicts.why: Client claimed $10 million; IRS valued at $3 million. $10M is 333% of $3M, exceeding 200%.
§ 6662(h)(2)(A)(i) defines gross valuation misstatement as claimed value ≥ 200% of correct value.
§ 6662(h) provides 40% penalty for gross valuation misstatement on charitable contribution property.

claims: The IRS currently takes up to 16 weeks to process amended returns
It can take up to 3 weeks from the date an amended return is filed for it to show up in the IRS system

verdicts.why: IRS publications state processing amended returns can take up to 16 weeks.
IRS publications state up to 3 weeks for amended return to show up in system.

claims: Interest on construction loans must be capitalized for self-produced assets
Under Section 263A(f), interest must be capitalized when it has been paid or incurred during the production period
The production period begins on the first date that any physical production activity is performed, such as clearing or excavating land
The production period ends when the property is placed into service and all production activities are completed

verdicts.why: 26 U.S.C. § 263A(f) requires capitalization of interest for self-produced assets including real property.
T.C. Memo. 2013-52 states Section 263A(f) requires capitalization when interest is paid or incurred during production period.
T.C. Memo. 2013-52 defines production period beginning on first date of physical production activity like clearing or excavating land.
T.C. Memo. 2013-52 states production period ends when property is placed into service and all production activities are completed.

claims: The maximum first-year depreciation deduction for a passenger automobile placed in service in 2025, for which Code section 168(k) additional first-year depreciation deduction applies, is $20,200
The maximum first-year depreciation deduction for a passenger automobile placed in service in 2025 that does not qualify for additional first-year depreciation is $12,200

verdicts.why: IRS Pub 463 (2025), p. 1 states the first-year depreciation limit is $20,200 for cars with Code section 168(k) additional first-year depreciation deduction.
IRS Pub 463 (2025), p. 24 states the first-year depreciation limit is $12,200 for cars without Code section 168(k) additional first-year depreciation deduction.
